decks.title: Immunity, AIDS and Substance Abuse — Part 1: Immunity
goals: Describe the physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine barriers of innate immunity
Distinguish active and passive, and humoral and cell-mediated, immunity; name the lymphoid organs
Describe antibody structure and the five classes of antibodies

slides.heading: Immunity
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how the body defends itself, from barriers we are born with to the targeted, remembering response we acquire.

visual.alt: Flow from innate immunity to acquired immunity to vaccination

slides.narration: Immunity is the ability of the body to fight disease-causing organisms. Some defences are present from birth and act against anything foreign. Others develop after we meet a particular pathogen, and remember it the next time.

slides.heading: Innate immunity: four kinds of barrier
slides.body_md: **Innate immunity** is **non-specific** and present **at birth**.

rows: Skin; mucus lining the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts traps microbes
Acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth, tears from the eyes
Leucocytes: neutrophils (PMNL), monocytes, natural killer cells; macrophages in tissues engulf microbes
Virus-infected cells release interferons that protect nearby cells

visual.alt: Table of the four barriers of innate immunity

slides.narration: The skin is the main physical barrier. Acid in the stomach and enzymes in saliva and tears destroy microbes. White blood cells and macrophages swallow invaders, and infected cells send chemical signals that warn their neighbours.

slides.heading: Interferons
slides.body_md: **Interferons** are proteins secreted by **virus-infected cells**. They act on **neighbouring, uninfected cells**, making them **resistant to further viral infection**. They are an example of the **cytokine barrier**.

rows: α-interferon as a biological response modifier, for example in cancer therapy

visual.alt: Table about interferons

slides.narration: An infected cell may die, but before it does it releases interferons. These warn the cells around it, which then make proteins that stop the virus from multiplying if it arrives.

slides.heading: Acquired immunity and memory
slides.body_md: **Acquired immunity** is **specific** and has **memory**. The first encounter gives a **primary response** of **low intensity**; a later encounter with the same pathogen gives a highly intensified **secondary (anamnestic) response**.

slides.narration: After the first exposure, antibody levels rise slowly and stay low. Memory cells remain, so after a second exposure the response is faster and many times stronger. That memory is the basis of vaccination.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: comparing the two responses
slides.body_md: From the graph, read the peak antibody levels of the primary and secondary responses, and find how many times stronger the secondary response is.
bullets: Primary peak ≈ **19** units (days 0–39); secondary peak ≈ **108** units (days 40–70).
Ratio $= \dfrac{108}{19} \approx 5.7$.
The secondary response also **rises much faster**, because **memory B and T cells** are ready.

visual.alt: Worked table: secondary response about 5.7 times the primary

slides.narration: Reading the two peaks and dividing shows the second response is several times stronger, and it peaks within days rather than weeks. A vaccine aims to give us the first, mild response so that the real infection meets the strong second one.

slides.heading: Humoral and cell-mediated immunity
slides.body_md: Acquired immunity is carried out by two kinds of **lymphocytes**.

rows: Antibodies in blood and lymph neutralise antigens
T-cells attack infected cells and help B-cells

visual.alt: Table comparing humoral and cell-mediated immunity

slides.narration: B-cells release antibodies into body fluids, hence the name humoral. T-cells act directly. Because the body can tell self from non-self, a transplanted organ from a poorly matched donor is attacked by T-cells and rejected.

slides.heading: Active and passive immunity
slides.body_md: Immunity can be produced by the body itself or given ready-made.

rows: Made by the person’s own body
Colostrum (IgA), placenta (IgG), injected antitoxin or antivenom

visual.alt: Table comparing active and passive immunity

slides.narration: A child who has measles, or is vaccinated against it, develops active immunity. A baby fed colostrum, or a snake-bite victim given antivenom, receives passive immunity: immediate but temporary protection.

slides.heading: Lymphoid organs
slides.body_md: **Lymphoid organs** are where lymphocytes form, mature and meet antigens.

rows: Lymphocytes are produced and mature into antigen-sensitive cells
Spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer’s patches of the small intestine, appendix
Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue of the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts
About half the lymphoid tissue of the body

visual.alt: Table of primary and secondary lymphoid organs

slides.narration: All lymphocytes are made in the bone marrow. T-cells mature in the thymus, which is large at birth and shrinks with age. Mature lymphocytes then move to secondary organs, such as lymph nodes and the spleen, where they meet antigens.

slides.heading: Quick check: passive immunity
slides.body_md: Which is an example of passive immunity?
slides.narration: Quick check. Who made the antibodies: the person, or someone else?

slides.heading: Antibody structure
slides.body_md: Each **antibody** is a **Y-shaped** protein of **four polypeptide chains**: **two heavy (H)** and **two light (L)** chains joined by **disulfide bonds** — written **H₂L₂**. The tips of the arms are the **antigen-binding sites**.

visual.alt: Y-shaped antibody with two heavy and two light chains

slides.narration: The two arms of the Y each bind an antigen, so one antibody can link two antigen particles. The stem determines the class of the antibody and how it interacts with other cells.

slides.heading: Five classes of antibodies
slides.body_md: Antibodies (immunoglobulins) are of five classes.

rows: Most abundant in blood (about 75–80 percent); monomer
Crosses the placenta; protects the foetus; secondary response
In secretions: colostrum, saliva, tears, mucus; often a dimer
Protects body surfaces and the newborn’s gut
First antibody made in a primary response
Antigen receptor that helps activate B-cells
Least abundant; bound to mast cells
Allergic reactions; defence against parasitic worms

visual.alt: Table of the five antibody classes with occurrence and function

slides.narration: Remember them as G for the general blood antibody that crosses the placenta, A in secretions, M made first and largest, D on B-cells, and E in allergy and worm infections.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting chains
slides.body_md: An IgM molecule is a pentamer of five basic antibody units, and secretory IgA is a dimer. How many heavy and light chains does each contain?
bullets: Each unit is $\mathrm{H_{2}L_{2}}$: 2 heavy + 2 light chains.
IgM: $5 \times 2 = 10$ heavy and 10 light chains, 20 in all.
IgA dimer: $2 \times 2 = 4$ heavy and 4 light chains, 8 in all.

visual.alt: Worked table: IgM has 20 chains

slides.narration: Multiply the number of basic units by two heavy and two light chains each. With ten antigen-binding arms, a single IgM molecule is very good at clumping antigens together, which suits its role early in an infection.

slides.heading: Vaccination, immunisation and autoimmunity
slides.body_md: **Vaccination** introduces **inactivated or weakened pathogens** or their **antigenic proteins**, producing antibodies and **memory B and T cells**. **Immunisation** may be **active** (vaccines) or **passive** (ready-made antibodies such as anti-tetanus serum). **Autoimmunity** is when the immune system attacks **self** cells, as in **rheumatoid arthritis**.

rows: Polio, measles, BCG; recombinant hepatitis B vaccine made in yeast
Antitoxin for tetanus; antivenom for snake bite

visual.alt: Table of vaccination, immunisation and autoimmunity examples

slides.narration: A vaccine trains the immune system with a harmless version of the pathogen, so the real one meets a strong secondary response. Sometimes, because of genetic and other causes, the immune system loses its tolerance of self and attacks the body’s own cells.

slides.heading: Quick check: antibody classes
slides.body_md: Which antibody crosses the placenta?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is the most abundant antibody in blood.

slides.heading: Quick check: interferons
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about interferons.
slides.narration: Quick check. Do interferons protect the infected cell, or its neighbours?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Innate: physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine (interferon) barriers.
Acquired: specific, with memory; primary (low) and secondary (strong, fast) responses.
Humoral (B-cells, antibodies) and cell-mediated (T-cells; graft rejection); active vs passive immunity.
Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow, thymus; secondary: spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer’s patches, appendix, MALT.
Antibody H₂L₂; IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, IgE; vaccination, immunisation, autoimmunity.

visual.alt: Summary table of antibody classes

slides.narration: To recap: innate barriers stop most invaders, and acquired immunity adds specific, remembered responses through B-cells and T-cells. Five classes of antibody play different roles, and vaccination uses immune memory to protect us.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **one example** for each of the four innate barriers.
Compare **active vs passive** and **humoral vs cell-mediated** in table form.
Draw the **antibody** with heavy and light chains, disulfide bonds and binding sites.
Match each **Ig class** to its occurrence and function.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn an example for each innate barrier. Compare the kinds of acquired immunity in a table. Practise drawing and labelling an antibody. And link each antibody class to where it is found and what it does.

slides.heading: AIDS and substance abuse
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a virus that destroys the immune system, and substances that damage body and mind.

visual.alt: Flow from HIV infection to loss of helper T-cells to opportunistic infections to prevention

slides.narration: AIDS is not present at birth; it is acquired. It weakens the immune system by destroying the very cells that coordinate it. Drugs, alcohol and tobacco cause a different kind of harm, but both problems are best tackled by awareness and prevention.

slides.heading: AIDS and HIV
slides.body_md: **AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome)**, first reported in **1981**, is caused by **HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus)**, a **retrovirus** with an **RNA** genome. There is a long **incubation period**, from a few months to many years (usually 5–10).

rows: Sexual contact with an infected person
Infected mother to child through the placenta

visual.alt: Table of ways HIV is and is not spread

slides.narration: People at higher risk include those with multiple sexual partners, drug users who share needles, and those needing repeated blood transfusions. HIV does not spread by everyday contact, so people living with HIV should not be shunned.

slides.heading: Replication of HIV in the host
slides.body_md: HIV enters **macrophages** and **helper T-lymphocytes (T_H cells)**. **Reverse transcriptase** copies its RNA into **viral DNA**, which is **integrated** into the host DNA. The infected cell then makes new viruses. Macrophages keep producing virus (an **HIV factory**), while helper T-cells are **destroyed**.

slides.narration: Because the virus writes its genes into the host’s own DNA, the infection cannot be cleared. As helper T-cells fall in number, the whole immune response weakens, and the patient falls ill with infections that a healthy person would resist.

slides.heading: Course of the disease
slides.body_md: As **helper T-cell numbers fall**, the person suffers **fever, diarrhoea and weight loss**, and then **opportunistic infections**.

rows: Few or no symptoms; HIV multiplies
Helper T-cell count falls slowly over years
Very low helper T-cell count; infections by Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and Toxoplasma
Anti-retroviral drugs prolong life but do not cure

visual.alt: Table of the course of HIV infection

slides.narration: Opportunistic infections are caused by microbes that are normally kept in check. With the immune system weakened, tuberculosis, fungal infections and parasites like Toxoplasma can take hold.

slides.heading: Diagnosis by ELISA
slides.body_md: **ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay)** detects **antibodies against HIV** in the blood. Antibodies bound in a well are revealed by an **enzyme-linked** second antibody that turns a substrate **coloured**; more colour means more antibody.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading an ELISA
slides.body_md: Two negative controls gave absorbance 0.07 and 0.09. The cut-off is 3 × their mean. Six samples gave 0.11, 1.32, 0.08, 0.95, 0.24, 1.47. Which are positive?
bullets: Mean of negatives $= \dfrac{0.07 + 0.09}{2} = 0.08$; cut-off $= 3 \times 0.08 = 0.24$.
Samples **above 0.24**: **S2, S4, S6** are positive.
S5 (0.24) equals the cut-off but does not exceed it, so it is **not positive**; it would be retested.

slides.heading: Prevention of AIDS
slides.body_md: There is **no cure** for AIDS, so **prevention** is the best option.

rows: Prevents spread among drug users and in clinics
Safe sex; free distribution of condoms
Awareness (NACO, NGOs; World AIDS Day, 1 December)

visual.alt: Table of measures to prevent AIDS

slides.narration: The National AIDS Control Organisation and many non-governmental organisations educate people about AIDS. Safe blood, sterile needles and safe sex break the main routes of spread.

slides.heading: Quick check: HIV
slides.body_md: Which enzyme does HIV use to copy its RNA genome into DNA?
slides.narration: Quick check. Its name says that it reverses transcription.

slides.heading: Drugs of abuse
slides.body_md: Many drugs that are useful medicines are **misused** for their effects on the nervous system.

rows: Morphine from the latex of the poppy, Papaver somniferum
Depressant; binds opioid receptors in the brain and gut; slows body functions
Bind cannabinoid receptors in the brain; affect the heart and circulation
Stimulant; interferes with dopamine transport; euphoria; hallucinations in excess
Prescribed for depression and insomnia; addictive when misused

visual.alt: Table of drugs of abuse with sources and effects

slides.narration: Heroin slows the body down, cocaine speeds it up, and cannabinoids alter perception and affect the heart. Medicines such as barbiturates help patients with insomnia or depression, but taken without medical supervision they become drugs of abuse.

slides.heading: Alcohol and smoking
slides.body_md: Alcohol and tobacco are legal but cause great harm.

rows: Damages the liver (cirrhosis) and nervous system; heavy use in pregnancy harms the foetus; accidents and violence
Nicotine stimulates release of adrenaline and noradrenaline, raising blood pressure and heart rate
Cancers of lung, throat and bladder; bronchitis, emphysema, heart disease, gastric ulcer
Binds haemoglobin, so less oxygen is carried

visual.alt: Table of effects of alcohol and smoking

slides.narration: Nicotine raises blood pressure and heart rate, and smoke delivers carbon monoxide and carcinogens to the lungs. Chewing tobacco raises the risk of mouth cancer. Alcohol, used heavily for years, scars the liver and damages nerves.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: pack-years
slides.body_md: Doctors measure smoking exposure in **pack-years** = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked. A man smoked 15 cigarettes a day for 20 years. Find his pack-years.
bullets: Packs per day $= \dfrac{15}{20} = 0.75$.
Pack-years $= 0.75 \times 20 = 15$.
The risk of lung cancer and heart disease rises with pack-years; stopping smoking lowers it over time.

visual.alt: Worked table: 15 pack-years

slides.narration: A pack holds twenty cigarettes, so fifteen a day is three quarters of a pack. Over twenty years that is fifteen pack-years, a level linked with a clearly raised risk of lung disease.

slides.heading: Addiction: reasons, dependence and prevention
slides.body_md: Most users first try drugs, alcohol or tobacco in **adolescence**. Repeated use leads to **addiction** and **dependence**; stopping suddenly causes **withdrawal symptoms**.

rows: Avoid undue peer pressure; let children follow their own interests
Peer pressure; wish to look “grown up”
Education and counselling about the effects
Escape from stress, failure or family problems
Seek help from parents and trusted peers
Watch for danger signs; professional and medical help, de-addiction centres

visual.alt: Table of reasons for addiction and measures for prevention

slides.narration: Danger signs include falling grades, withdrawal from family and friends, and changes in sleep and appetite. Parents and teachers who notice early, and who listen rather than blame, can help a young person get counselling and medical help.

slides.heading: Quick check: drugs
slides.body_md: Which drug is obtained from the latex of the poppy plant?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is processed into heroin.

slides.heading: Quick check: smoking
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about smoking.
slides.narration: Quick check. What does carbon monoxide do to haemoglobin?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: AIDS: HIV, a retrovirus; spread by sex, blood, needles, mother to child; not by touch.
HIV: reverse transcriptase, integration into host DNA; macrophages as HIV factories; helper T-cells destroyed; opportunistic infections.
Diagnosis by ELISA; prevention by safe blood, disposable needles, safe sex, awareness (NACO).
Opioids (poppy), cannabinoids (Cannabis), cocaine (coca), barbiturates; alcohol and tobacco.
Addiction begins in adolescence; prevent by education, counselling, family support and medical help.

visual.alt: Summary table of substances and sources

slides.narration: To recap: HIV destroys helper T-cells and is diagnosed by ELISA, and prevention depends on safe practices and awareness. Drugs, alcohol and tobacco have specific sources and damaging effects, and addiction is best prevented through education and support.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Describe **HIV replication** in steps, naming **reverse transcriptase** and **helper T-cells**.
State **ELISA** in full and what it detects.
Give **source and effect** for each drug.
List **reasons** for addiction and **measures** to prevent it.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Describe how HIV multiplies, step by step. Expand ELISA and say what it detects. Give the source and effect of each drug. And learn the reasons for addiction alongside the ways to prevent it.

sections.heading: 1. Innate immunity
sections.body_md:
**Immunity** is the overall ability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms. **Innate immunity** is **non-specific** and **present at birth**. It consists of four kinds of barriers:
1. **Physical barriers** — **skin** prevents entry of microbes; **mucus** lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts traps microbes.
2. **Physiological barriers** — **acid in the stomach**, **saliva** in the mouth and **tears** from the eyes prevent microbial growth.
3. **Cellular barriers** — certain **leucocytes**: **polymorpho-nuclear leucocytes (PMNL-neutrophils)**, **monocytes** and **natural killer** lymphocytes in blood, and **macrophages** in tissues, **phagocytose** and destroy microbes.
4. **Cytokine barriers** — **virus-infected cells** secrete proteins called **interferons**, which protect **non-infected cells** from further viral infection.

**Interferons** limit the spread of viruses; α-interferon is also used as a biological response modifier in cancer treatment.

key_terms.definition_md: Proteins secreted by virus-infected cells that protect neighbouring cells from viral infection.
Engulfing and destroying of microbes by cells such as macrophages.

visual.alt: Table of innate barriers with examples

sections.heading: 2. Acquired immunity and lymphoid organs
sections.body_md:
**Acquired immunity** is **pathogen-specific** and is characterised by **memory**. The first encounter produces a **primary response** of **low intensity**; a subsequent encounter with the same pathogen produces a highly intensified **secondary (anamnestic) response** (in the model graph, peaks of about 19 and 108 units).

Two kinds of **lymphocytes** carry it out:
- **B-lymphocytes** produce **antibodies** into blood and lymph — **humoral (antibody-mediated) immune response**.
- **T-lymphocytes** do not secrete antibodies but help B-cells and attack infected cells — **cell-mediated immunity (CMI)**. CMI is responsible for **graft rejection**: the body distinguishes **self from non-self**, so tissue and blood-group matching are essential before transplants, and patients take **immunosuppressants**.

**Active immunity** — the host’s own body produces antibodies on exposure to antigens (live or dead microbes or proteins), by **natural infection** or **vaccination**; it is **slow** but **long-lasting**.
**Passive immunity** — **ready-made antibodies** are given: **colostrum** supplies **IgA** to the newborn; the foetus receives **IgG** through the **placenta**; injected **antitoxins** (tetanus) and **antivenom** (snake bite). It is **immediate** but **short-lived**.

**Lymphoid organs:** **primary** — **bone marrow** (all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced) and **thymus** (T-lymphocytes mature; it is large at birth and shrinks with age); lymphocytes become antigen-sensitive here. **Secondary** — **spleen** (filters blood, reservoir of erythrocytes), **lymph nodes** (trap microbes in lymph), **tonsils**, **Peyer’s patches** of the small intestine and the **appendix**; here lymphocytes interact with antigens and proliferate. **MALT** (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) lines the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts and makes up about **50 percent** of lymphoid tissue.

key_terms.definition_md: Specific defence that develops after exposure and has memory.
Defence by T-lymphocytes; responsible for graft rejection.

sections.heading: 3. Antibodies, vaccination and autoimmunity
sections.body_md:
**Antibody structure:** each antibody molecule has **four polypeptide chains** — **two heavy** and **two light** — joined by **disulfide bonds**, written **H₂L₂**. The molecule is **Y-shaped**; the tips of its arms are **antigen-binding sites**.

**Classes of antibodies (immunoglobulins):**
- **IgG** — most abundant in serum (about 75–80 percent); monomer; **crosses the placenta**, giving passive immunity to the foetus; main antibody of the secondary response.
- **IgA** — in body **secretions**: **colostrum**, saliva, tears, mucus; usually a dimer; protects body surfaces and the newborn’s gut.
- **IgM** — **pentamer** (5 units, 20 chains), the largest; **first** antibody formed in a primary response; efficient at agglutination.
- **IgD** — on the **surface of B-cells**; acts as an **antigen receptor** that helps activate B-cells.
- **IgE** — least abundant; binds **mast cells** and basophils; involved in **allergic reactions** and defence against **parasitic worms**.

**Vaccination and immunisation:** a vaccine is a preparation of **antigenic proteins** of a pathogen or **inactivated/weakened** pathogen. It generates antibodies and **memory B and T cells**, so the real pathogen meets a rapid, intense secondary response. **Recombinant DNA technology** produces antigenic polypeptides in bacteria or yeast (for example the **hepatitis B vaccine** made in yeast). **Active immunisation** uses vaccines; **passive immunisation** gives pre-formed antibodies or antitoxins (tetanus antitoxin, snake antivenom) when a quick response is needed.

**Autoimmunity:** due to genetic and other unknown reasons, the body sometimes attacks **self-cells**, resulting in damage — **autoimmune diseases** such as **rheumatoid arthritis**.

Most abundant antibody; crosses the placenta.
Preparation of antigens that induces immunity and memory.
Immune attack on the body’s own cells.

sections.heading: 4. AIDS
sections.body_md:
**AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome)** is a deficiency of the immune system acquired during life; first reported in **1981**, it has spread worldwide. It is caused by **HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus)**, a **retrovirus** with an **RNA** genome and an envelope.

**Transmission:** (a) **sexual contact** with an infected person; (b) **transfusion of contaminated blood** and blood products; (c) **sharing infected needles** (intravenous drug users); (d) from **infected mother to child through the placenta**. It does **not** spread by touch or physical contact. There is a long **incubation period** (a few months to many years, usually 5–10).

**Replication of HIV:** the virus enters **macrophages**, where its **RNA** is copied into **viral DNA** by **reverse transcriptase**. The viral DNA is **integrated into the host cell’s DNA** and directs the infected cell to make virus particles; the macrophage continues to produce virus — an **HIV factory**. HIV also enters **helper T-lymphocytes (T_H)**, replicates and produces progeny viruses that attack other helper T-cells. The **number of helper T-lymphocytes falls progressively**; the patient has **fever, diarrhoea and weight loss**, and becomes prone to **opportunistic infections** by bacteria (*Mycobacterium*), viruses, fungi and parasites such as *Toxoplasma*.

**Diagnosis:** **ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay)** detects antibodies against HIV; the colour produced in a well is compared with a cut-off from negative controls.

**Treatment and prevention:** **anti-retroviral drugs** are only partially effective, prolonging life. Prevention: **NACO** and NGOs educate people; **blood is screened** in blood banks; **disposable needles and syringes**; **free distribution of condoms**; avoiding drug abuse; regular check-ups for susceptible groups; **World AIDS Day** on **1 December**.

Infection by microbes that a healthy immune system would control.
Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay; used to detect HIV antibodies.

sections.heading: 5. Alcohol, smoking and drugs
sections.body_md:
**Commonly abused drugs:**
- **Opioids** bind **opioid receptors** in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. **Heroin** (“smack”, **diacetylmorphine**) is a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound made by acetylation of **morphine**, extracted from the **latex of the poppy, *Papaver somniferum***. It is a **depressant** and slows down body functions.
- **Cannabinoids** interact with **cannabinoid receptors** in the brain. Natural cannabinoids come from the **inflorescences of *Cannabis sativa***; marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja are inhaled or taken orally and affect the **cardiovascular system**.
- **Cocaine** (coke, crack) comes from the **coca plant, *Erythroxylum coca***, native to South America. It **interferes with the transport of dopamine** and has a potent **stimulating** action on the CNS, producing euphoria and increased energy; excessive doses cause **hallucinations**.
- **Barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines** and similar drugs, normally used as medicines for **depression and insomnia**, are often abused. Plants such as *Atropa belladonna* and *Datura* have hallucinogenic properties.

**Tobacco and smoking:** tobacco contains **nicotine**, an alkaloid that stimulates the **adrenal gland** to release **adrenaline and noradrenaline**, raising **blood pressure and heart rate**. Smoking is associated with cancers of the **lung, urinary bladder and throat**, **bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease** and **gastric ulcer**; tobacco chewing with **oral cancer**. Smoke raises **carbon monoxide** in blood, reducing the oxygen carried by haemoglobin.

**Alcohol:** chronic use damages the **nervous system** and **liver (cirrhosis)**; use during pregnancy harms the **foetus**.

**Adolescence and addiction:** reasons include **curiosity, adventure, excitement, experimentation**, **peer pressure**, escape from **stress and failure**, family history and the false perception that it is “cool”. Repeated use causes **addiction** (psychological attachment) and **dependence**: when intake is stopped abruptly, **withdrawal syndrome** (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating) appears.

**Prevention and control:** avoid **undue peer pressure**; **education and counselling**; **seek help from parents and peers**; look for **danger signs** (falling grades, withdrawal, changes in sleep and appetite); **professional and medical help** from de-addiction and rehabilitation centres.

Unpleasant symptoms when a dependent person stops a drug abruptly.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling interferons antibodies (they are cytokines from virus-infected cells).
- Saying T-cells make antibodies (B-cells do; T-cells mediate CMI).
- Mixing primary (bone marrow, thymus) and secondary lymphoid organs.
- Saying IgA crosses the placenta (IgG does; IgA is in colostrum).
- Saying HIV is spread by touch or mosquitoes.
- Calling heroin a stimulant (it is a depressant; cocaine is the stimulant).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a barrier, a lymphoid organ, an antibody class, a drug source, ELISA in full.
- 2–3-mark questions: active vs passive; humoral vs CMI; antibody diagram; HIV replication; effects of smoking.
- 5-mark questions in parts: immunity with the response graph; antibody classes; AIDS from cause to prevention; drugs and adolescence.

questions.stem_md: Patients with severe burns over much of the body are very likely to suffer infections. Which barrier of innate immunity have they lost?

options.text_md: The physical barrier of intact skin
The physiological barrier of stomach acid
The cellular barrier of macrophages in the spleen

questions.solution_md: Skin is the main physical barrier; burns remove it — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Years of smoking damage the mucus-lined airways of a man, and he now catches chest infections often. Which defence has been weakened?

options.text_md: The physical barrier formed by mucus that traps microbes in the respiratory tract

questions.solution_md: Mucus lining the airways traps microbes — a physical barrier of innate immunity — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Interferons help to limit the spread of a viral infection in the body.

**Reason (R):** Interferons are secreted by virus-infected cells and protect neighbouring non-infected cells from further viral infection.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the protection of neighbouring cells explains how spread is limited — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Lymphocytes of innate immunity that kill virus-infected and tumour cells without needing antibodies are called natural ______ cells.
Give a reason: tears are regarded as part of the innate immune system.

answer.model_answer_md: Tears are a **physiological barrier**: they **wash away** and help **destroy microbes** entering the eye.

marking_scheme.step: Physiological barrier that removes or kills microbes

questions.stem_md: Name the four types of barriers of innate immunity and give one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Physical** — skin or mucus of the airways and gut. **Physiological** — acid in the stomach, saliva or tears. **Cellular** — neutrophils, monocytes, natural killer cells or macrophages. **Cytokine** — interferons secreted by virus-infected cells.

questions.stem_md: A kidney transplanted from a poorly matched donor is attacked and rejected by the recipient. Which part of the immune system is mainly responsible?

options.text_md: The physical barrier of the skin

questions.solution_md: Graft rejection is due to cell-mediated immunity, which recognises non-self — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A newborn baby fed on colostrum in the first days after birth becomes protected against some infections. What kind of immunity is this?

options.text_md: Active immunity from the baby’s own antibodies
Artificial active immunity from a vaccine
Natural passive immunity from IgA antibodies in the colostrum

questions.solution_md: Ready-made IgA antibodies are received from the mother — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In which organ do T-lymphocytes mature into antigen-sensitive cells?
questions.solution_md: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where T-cells mature — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which secondary lymphoid organ filters blood, trapping blood-borne microbes, and acts as a reservoir of red blood cells?
During a throat infection, small swellings appear in the neck and become tender. What is happening in them?

options.text_md: The thymus is producing new red blood cells.
Antibodies are being made by the skin.
Interferons are being stored for later use.
Lymph nodes are trapping microbes, and lymphocytes there are multiplying in response.

questions.solution_md: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where lymphocytes meet antigens and proliferate — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A farmer bitten by a cobra is injected with antivenom rather than a vaccine. Why?

options.text_md: A vaccine would give only passive immunity.
Antivenom supplies ready-made antibodies at once, whereas a vaccine would take too long to act.
Antivenom makes the farmer produce memory cells.

questions.solution_md: Passive immunisation acts immediately, which is vital for venom — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Children receive a booster dose of a vaccine some months after the first dose. What is the main benefit?

options.text_md: It gives passive immunity from the mother.
It triggers a faster, stronger secondary response from memory cells.

questions.solution_md: Re-exposure to the antigen produces the intensified secondary response — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Tissue matching is carried out before an organ transplant.

**Reason (R):** The immune system can distinguish self from non-self, and T-cells attack foreign tissue.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the self–non-self recognition explains why matching is needed — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between active and passive immunity, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Active immunity:** the person’s **own body makes antibodies** after infection or **vaccination**; it develops **slowly** but **lasts long** — for example, after a measles vaccine. **Passive immunity:** **ready-made antibodies** are received; it acts **at once** but is **short-lived** — for example, **IgA in colostrum** or an injected **antitoxin**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between humoral immunity and cell-mediated immunity.

answer.model_answer_md: **Humoral immunity** is carried out by **B-lymphocytes**, which secrete **antibodies** into blood and lymph that neutralise antigens. **Cell-mediated immunity** is carried out by **T-lymphocytes**, which do not secrete antibodies but **attack infected or foreign cells** and help B-cells; it causes **graft rejection**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between primary and secondary lymphoid organs, naming two of each, and state what MALT is.

answer.model_answer_md: **Primary lymphoid organs** — **bone marrow** and **thymus** — are where lymphocytes are **produced and mature** into antigen-sensitive cells. **Secondary lymphoid organs** — such as the **spleen**, **lymph nodes**, **tonsils**, **Peyer’s patches** and **appendix** — are where mature lymphocytes **meet antigens and proliferate**. **MALT** is **mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue** lining the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts; it makes up about **half** of the body’s lymphoid tissue.

questions.stem_md: The figure shows antibody levels after two exposures to the same antigen, on day 0 and day 40. The peaks are about 19 and 108 units. Explain the difference in the two responses and how a vaccine makes use of it.

answer.model_answer_md: The first exposure gives a **primary response**: antibody levels rise **slowly** to a **low** peak (about 19). It also leaves **memory B and T cells**. On the **second exposure**, these memory cells respond **quickly**, giving a **secondary (anamnestic) response** that rises fast to a much **higher** peak (about 108). A **vaccine** provides the first exposure **safely**, so that a real infection later meets the strong secondary response.

marking_scheme.step: Primary: slow, low; memory cells formed

questions.stem_md: Patient A receives a kidney from an identical twin; patient B receives one from an unrelated, poorly matched donor. B’s kidney is rejected unless he takes immunosuppressant drugs, which also make him prone to infections. Explain all three observations.

answer.model_answer_md: An **identical twin** has the **same antigens**, so A’s immune system treats the kidney as **self** and does not attack it. B’s kidney carries **foreign (non-self) antigens**; **T-lymphocytes** recognise them and destroy it — **cell-mediated** graft rejection. **Immunosuppressants** reduce this response, but they **weaken immunity in general**, so B becomes **more prone to infections**.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between innate and acquired immunity. [1]
(b) Explain the primary and secondary immune responses with reference to memory. [2]
(c) Explain why a person bitten by a snake is given antivenom, while a child is given a vaccine against polio. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Innate immunity** is **non-specific** and present **at birth**; **acquired immunity** is **specific**, develops after exposure, and has **memory**.

(b) The **primary response** to the first encounter is **slow and of low intensity**, and leaves **memory B and T cells**. A later encounter with the same antigen triggers a **secondary (anamnestic) response** that is **faster and much stronger**.

(c) Venom acts **quickly**, so the victim needs **ready-made antibodies** at once — **passive immunisation**. A child is not yet infected, so a **vaccine** can safely produce **active immunity** with **long-lasting memory**.

questions.stem_md: Which antibody, a large pentamer, is the first to be produced during a primary immune response?
questions.solution_md: IgM appears first; IgG dominates the secondary response — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which antibody, the most abundant in blood serum, crosses the placenta to protect the foetus?
A child given the measles vaccine stays free of measles when an outbreak occurs at school years later. What does the vaccine leave in the child’s body that explains this?

options.text_md: Memory B and T cells specific to the measles antigen
A permanent fever that kills viruses
Extra skin layers that block viruses

questions.solution_md: Vaccination produces memory cells for a rapid secondary response — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an autoimmune disease, in which the body’s immune system attacks its own cells?
The hepatitis B vaccine is made by expressing the gene for a viral surface protein in yeast. What kind of vaccine is this?

options.text_md: A recombinant DNA vaccine made of an antigenic protein

questions.solution_md: Recombinant DNA technology produces the antigen in yeast — option (c).

**Assertion (A):** Heroin is a stimulant obtained from the coca plant.

**Reason (R):** Cocaine slows down body functions by binding opioid receptors.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: heroin is a depressant from the poppy; cocaine is a stimulant that interferes with dopamine transport — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An IgM molecule is a pentamer of five basic antibody units. How many polypeptide chains (heavy and light together) does one IgM molecule contain?

**Assertion (A):** IgD is found on the surface of B-lymphocytes.

**Reason (R):** IgE binds to mast cells and basophils.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the binding of IgE to mast cells does not explain where IgD is found; IgD acts as an antigen receptor on B-cells — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The antibody class found in colostrum, saliva, tears and mucus is Ig______.
Draw or describe the structure of an antibody molecule, naming its chains and bonds.

answer.model_answer_md: An antibody is a **Y-shaped** molecule of **four polypeptide chains**: **two heavy** chains forming the stem and inner arms and **two light** chains on the outer arms (**H₂L₂**), held together by **disulfide bonds**. The tips of the two arms are **antigen-binding sites**.

marking_scheme.step: Two heavy and two light chains

questions.stem_md: Name the antibody class most involved in each case and give a reason: (i) a newborn protected by its mother’s antibodies before birth; (ii) a breast-fed baby protected in the gut; (iii) a person who sneezes when exposed to pollen.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **IgG** — the most abundant antibody in the mother’s blood and the only class that **crosses the placenta**, so the foetus is born with ready-made protection. (ii) **IgA** — secreted into **colostrum** and breast milk, it coats and protects the **lining of the baby’s gut** against microbes. (iii) **IgE** — made against the pollen allergen, it binds **mast cells**, which release **histamine** and cause the **allergic** sneezing.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of an antibody molecule. [2]
(b) State the occurrence and function of IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD and IgE. [2]
(c) What is autoimmunity? Give one example. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** a **Y-shaped** molecule with **two heavy chains** and **two light chains**, **disulfide bonds** between chains, and **antigen-binding sites** at the tips of the arms.

(b) **IgG** — most abundant in serum; **crosses the placenta**. **IgA** — in **secretions and colostrum**; protects surfaces. **IgM** — **pentamer**; **first** in the primary response. **IgD** — on **B-cell surfaces**; antigen receptor. **IgE** — on **mast cells**; **allergy** and worm infections.

(c) **Autoimmunity** is an immune attack on the body’s **own cells**, for example **rheumatoid arthritis**.

questions.stem_md: The number of which cells falls progressively in a person infected with HIV?
questions.solution_md: HIV destroys helper T-cells, weakening the immune response — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Describe how HIV multiplies after entering the human body.

answer.model_answer_md: HIV first enters **macrophages**. Its **RNA genome** is copied into **viral DNA** by **reverse transcriptase**. The viral DNA is **integrated into the host cell’s DNA** and directs the cell to make new virus particles; the macrophage keeps producing virus (an **HIV factory**). HIV also enters **helper T-lymphocytes**, replicates, and its progeny attack more helper T-cells, whose **number falls progressively**.

questions.stem_md: State the principle of ELISA for diagnosing HIV infection. In one test the negative controls read 0.07 and 0.09, the cut-off is 3 × their mean, and three samples read 0.11, 1.32, 0.95. Which samples are positive?

answer.model_answer_md: ELISA is based on **antigen–antibody interaction**: HIV antigens fixed in a well bind **antibodies** in the patient’s serum, and an **enzyme-linked** second antibody produces a **colour**; more colour means more antibody. Cut-off = 3 × 0.08 = **0.24**. Samples **1.32 and 0.95** exceed it and are **positive**; 0.11 is **negative**.

questions.stem_md: Suggest three measures a state health department should take to reduce the spread of HIV, and explain how each breaks a route of transmission.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Screen all donated blood** in blood banks — prevents spread by **transfusion**. (ii) Ensure **disposable needles and syringes** in clinics and needle-exchange for drug users — prevents spread through **shared needles**. (iii) **Awareness campaigns** and **free distribution of condoms** — reduce **sexual transmission**; regular testing of high-risk groups and of pregnant women also reduces **mother-to-child** spread.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Expand AIDS and name its causative agent. List three ways in which it is transmitted. [2]
(b) Explain why a person with AIDS falls ill with infections that healthy people resist. [2]
(c) Name the test used to diagnose HIV infection. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome**, caused by **HIV**, a **retrovirus**. It spreads by **sexual contact** with an infected person, **transfusion of contaminated blood**, **sharing infected needles**, and from **mother to child** through the placenta.

(b) HIV multiplies in **helper T-lymphocytes** and destroys them, so their **number falls**. Helper T-cells coordinate both **humoral** and **cell-mediated** responses, so immunity **weakens**, and **opportunistic infections** (such as tuberculosis, fungal and Toxoplasma infections) take hold.

(c) **ELISA** (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay).

Name the plant source of (i) heroin, (ii) cocaine, (iii) marijuana and (iv) nicotine.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Heroin** — morphine from the latex of the **poppy, *Papaver somniferum***. (ii) **Cocaine** — the **coca plant, *Erythroxylum coca***. (iii) **Marijuana** — inflorescences of ***Cannabis sativa***. (iv) **Nicotine** — the **tobacco** plant (*Nicotiana*).

questions.stem_md: State two reasons why adolescents start using drugs or alcohol, and two danger signs parents should watch for.

answer.model_answer_md: **Reasons:** **curiosity** and the wish for adventure or excitement; **peer pressure**; escape from **stress or failure**; the false idea that it is “**cool**”. **Danger signs:** **falling grades** or absence from school, **withdrawal** from family and friends, changes in **sleep and appetite**, and **loss of interest** in hobbies.

questions.stem_md: A 45-year-old man who has smoked since college has a persistent cough, gets breathless climbing stairs, and has high blood pressure. Relate each problem to an effect of smoking.

answer.model_answer_md: **Persistent cough** — smoke irritates and damages the airways, causing **bronchitis**. **Breathlessness** — smoking destroys the walls of **alveoli** (**emphysema**), and **carbon monoxide** binds haemoglobin, reducing oxygen supply. **High blood pressure** — **nicotine** stimulates the release of **adrenaline and noradrenaline**, raising **blood pressure and heart rate**.

questions.stem_md: Compare opioids, cannabinoids and cocaine with respect to their source and their effect on the body.

answer.model_answer_md: **Opioids** (heroin) — from **morphine** in the latex of the **poppy**; bind **opioid receptors** in the brain and gut; a **depressant** that slows body functions. **Cannabinoids** (marijuana, hashish) — from ***Cannabis sativa***; bind **cannabinoid receptors** in the brain and affect the **heart and circulation**. **Cocaine** — from the **coca plant**; interferes with **dopamine** transport; a **stimulant** causing euphoria and, in excess, **hallucinations**.

(b) Describe two effects each of chronic alcohol use and of smoking. [2]
(c) What is withdrawal syndrome? [1]
(d) Suggest two ways in which schools can help prevent drug abuse among students. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Heroin is made from **morphine** in the latex of the **poppy (*Papaver somniferum*)**; it **slows down body functions** by binding opioid receptors, so it is a **depressant**.

(b) **Alcohol:** **liver cirrhosis**; damage to the **nervous system**; harm to the **foetus** in pregnancy. **Smoking:** **lung and throat cancer**, **bronchitis and emphysema**, **raised blood pressure** from nicotine, **less oxygen** carried because of carbon monoxide.

(c) Unpleasant symptoms — **anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating** — when a dependent person **stops** a drug **abruptly**.

(d) **Education and counselling** about the effects; **reducing peer pressure** through activities and mentors; teachers watching for **danger signs** and referring students for **help**.

questions.passage_md:
A volunteer received a first dose of a tetanus vaccine on day 0 and a booster on day 42. Antibody levels (arbitrary units) were measured:

| Day | 0 | 7 | 14 | 28 | 42 | 49 | 56 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Antibody level | 2 | 18 | 34 | 20 | 6 | 120 | 210 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 6.2

**(b)** (a) Memory cells formed after the first dose responded quickly.

**(c)** (i) He has **memory cells** against the tetanus antigen, so any toxin or bacteria entering the wound trigger a **rapid, strong secondary response**; **antibodies** neutralise the toxin **before** it can cause disease.

**OR** (ii) The serum gives **passive immunity**: ready-made antibodies act **at once** but **do not last** and leave **no memory**. The volunteer has **active immunity** with **memory**, which lasts for years.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{210}{34} = 6.2$.

**(b)** The secondary response depends on memory B and T cells — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Secondary response.

(ii) Passive vs active.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): An unvaccinated person with the same wound is given anti-tetanus serum. How does his protection differ from the volunteer’s?
